metadata.description: Ancient Witness Bestiary — textual dossiers from Hebrew Scripture, Dead Sea Scrolls, Apocrypha, and Pseudepigrapha
metadata.editorialMethod: Ancient testimony first. Attested traits are separated from inference; later Solomonic material is used only where the earlier record is silent.

entries.name: Michael

artReview.depictedWitness: Testament of Abraham, long recension, chapters 2-6
artReview.scene: At Mamre, Abraham washes the feet of the human-passing chief-captain Michael while Isaac attends; Michael's tears become precious stones in the basin.
crossTextualRestraints: No wings, halo, crown, armor, or weapon is supplied by this encounter
The radiant warrior-traveler form belongs to the Testament of Abraham and is not projected into Daniel
Martial rank is conveyed by bearing; mercy and grief are conveyed by the witnessed action
Later planetary colors, seals, and Solomonic insignia are excluded
artReview.style: Ancient Witness Bestiary: historically grounded narrative realism, encaustic and egg-tempera pigment character, tactile ancient materials, restrained sacred strangeness

roles: Prince Who Stands for Daniel's People
entries.description: Daniel calls Michael one of the chief princes and the great prince who stands for Daniel's people. Enoch's witnesses remember more than a warrior: Michael hears the earth's accusation, binds Semyaza, interprets mysteries, guards the elect portion of humankind, and trembles with mercy at severe judgment. Jude names him the archangel who refuses to condemn from his own authority; Revelation places him at the head of angels against the dragon. In the later Testament of Abraham he appears as God's radiant chief-captain, a beautiful young warrior who passes as a traveler, walks beside Abraham, weeps with the household, and receives Abraham's soul.

extraBiblical: War Scroll (1QM; Prince of Light identification is interpretive)
Testament of Abraham, recensions A and B

ancientDossier.witness: Daniel's messenger says Michael came to his aid against Persia's prince and identifies Michael as both one of the chief princes and the prince assigned to Daniel's people. The Enochic seer places him among the holy presences before the Lord of Spirits: he joins the appeal for a blood-soaked earth, receives the order to bind Semyaza, explains hidden things, and helps execute the last judgment. The Testament of Abraham makes him the chief-captain sent to prepare Abraham for death.
ancientDossier.attestedTraits: High but not solitary rank; special responsibility for Daniel's people and Enoch's elect portion of humanity; command within a heavenly host; delegated rather than self-originating authority; mercy, patience, grief at judgment, interpretation of visions, custody of a powerful oath, restraint toward the adversary, and care for the righteous dead. The Testament of Abraham alone supplies a visible apparition: youthful, extraordinarily beautiful, radiant like the sun, and warriorlike, yet able to pass as a human traveler. It calls him incorporeal while narrating his feet, tears, walking, and hospitality; his tears become precious stones.
ancientDossier.textualBoundary: The earliest named witnesses give Michael no wings, halo, armor, weapon, hair color, or facial anatomy. Daniel's radiant linen-clad figure is not named Michael and must not be used as his portrait. The War Scroll does not plainly write Michael's name where modern summaries identify the Prince of Light with him. Solar colors, planetary emblems, seals, and ritual weapons belong to later magical corpora and are excluded from this card. The visible form used by the artwork is specifically the later Testament of Abraham apparition and is not projected backward into Daniel or 1 Enoch.

entries.name: Gabriel

artReview.scene: At the Ulai, the manlike Gabriel touches and sets the fallen Daniel upright while the ram-and-goat vision recedes behind them.
crossTextualRestraints: No wings, halo, trumpet, lily, armor, or weapon is supplied by Daniel's encounter
Daniel 10's unnamed radiant linen-clad figure is not used as Gabriel's anatomy
The ram, goat, river, touch, and terrified seer anchor the image to Daniel 8
Later lunar, western, watery, and Solomonic correspondences are excluded
artReview.style: Ancient Witness Bestiary: historically grounded narrative realism, encaustic and egg-tempera pigment character, tactile ancient materials, restrained sacred strangeness

roles: Overseer of Powers, Paradise, Serpents, and Cherubim
entries.description: Daniel remembers Gabriel first as a manlike heavenly interpreter: he approaches the terrified seer at the Ulai, touches him, sets him upright, and gives wisdom concerning the appointed end. In Luke, Gabriel identifies himself as one who stands in God's presence and is sent to speak to Zechariah and Mary. The Enochic witnesses give him a sterner reach: he joins the appeal over a blood-soaked earth, turns the Watchers' offspring against one another, stands over all the powers, and is assigned Paradise, serpents, and cherubim. He is herald and interpreter, but also petitioner, guardian, and executor of delegated judgment.

ancientDossier.witness: At the Ulai, Daniel sees one with the appearance of a man; a voice names him Gabriel and commands him to make Daniel understand. Gabriel comes near, terrifies the seer, speaks, touches him, and sets him upright. He later reaches Daniel during prayer to give wisdom and understanding. In Luke he stands at the right of the incense altar, names himself as one who stands in God's presence, and is sent into Mary's dwelling at Nazareth. In 1 Enoch he sees humanity's bloodshed, brings its cause before the Most High, receives orders against the Watchers' children, and joins the fiery judgment of Azazel's hosts.
ancientDossier.attestedTraits: Manlike manifestation; immediate delegated access to God's presence; rapid arrival; intelligible speech; touch that restores a collapsed witness; interpretation, instruction, announcement, and correction. The Enochic record adds intercession, command over the Watchers' violent offspring, jurisdiction over all powers and over Paradise, serpents, and cherubim, and participation in final punishment. Later rabbinic reception remembers Gabriel as advocate, marker of judgment, prince of fire, and destroying messenger, but preserves conflicting accounts of his instruments.
ancientDossier.textualBoundary: No named early witness gives Gabriel wings, halo, trumpet, lily, armor, sword, complexion, hair, or clothing color. Daniel 9's difficult phrase about his swift arrival is not anatomical evidence for wings. Daniel 10's beryl-bodied, lightning-faced, fire-eyed linen figure is never named Gabriel. The furnace rescue and other identifications of unnamed biblical messengers belong to later rabbinic reception. Western, lunar, watery, colored, perfumed, and sigilic assignments are late magical systems and are excluded from the core portrait.

entries.name: Raphael

artReview.scene: Raphael, passing as the hired traveler Azariah, instructs Tobias beside the seized fish on the Tigris while their dog and journey gear remain nearby.
crossTextualRestraints: No wings, halo, medical emblem, glowing staff, armor, or potion apparatus is supplied by Tobit
Raphael must pass completely as a young human traveler until his later disclosure
Fish, riverbank, dog, and travel gear anchor the image to Tobit's narrative
Later planetary, directional, colored, and Solomonic correspondences are excluded
artReview.style: Ancient Witness Bestiary: historically grounded narrative realism, encaustic and egg-tempera pigment character, tactile ancient materials, restrained sacred strangeness

roles: Interpreter of the Dead and Eden
entries.description: In Tobit, Raphael answers two desperate prayers by passing as the hired kinsman Azariah: he walks with Tobias, instructs him at the Tigris, arranges his marriage, binds Asmodeus, recovers family money, and directs the cure of Tobit's blinded eyes. Only at the end does he reveal that he presented their prayers and is one of the seven who stand before God. In 1 Enoch he hears the blood-soaked earth, binds Azazel beneath jagged stones, heals the corruption the Watchers caused, guides Enoch among the waiting dead, and stands over human spirits, diseases, and wounds.

extraBiblical: Jubilees 10:7-13 (unnamed healing angel; Raphael identification is editorial)

ancientDossier.witness: Tobit and Sarah pray for death; God sends Raphael to heal them both. Appearing as the young kinsman Azariah, he accepts hire, travels on foot, instructs Tobias to seize and open the Tigris fish, explains its medicines, binds Asmodeus in Upper Egypt, conducts family business, and directs Tobit's eye cure. He then reveals that he carried their prayers before God and belongs to the seven who stand ready before divine glory. Enoch's seer sees the same named angel receive the command to bind Azazel and heal the injured earth.
ancientDossier.attestedTraits: A wholly human-passing young traveler; guide, negotiator, companion, prayer-bearer, healer, demon-binder, and custodian/interpreter of human spirits. His remedies use ordinary-looking matter—fish heart, liver, and gall—under divine commission. His healing includes restraining the agent of harm: Asmodeus is bound far away, and Azazel is buried under rough stones and darkness. His authority is delegated, practical, and often concealed until the work is complete.
ancientDossier.textualBoundary: Tobit gives Raphael no wings, halo, staff, medical emblem, armor, complexion, or clothing color. The dog accompanies the travelers in major textual forms but is not Raphael's symbolic animal. Jubilees 10 does not name its medicine-teaching angel; identifying him as Raphael is an editorial comparison. Later assignments to directions, elements, planets, colors, seals, and incenses belong to inconsistent magical systems and are excluded from the early portrait.

entries.name: Uriel

artReview.scene: Uriel shows and records for Enoch the ordered courses, names, seasons, and portals of the luminaries at the ends of the earth.
crossTextualRestraints: No early named witness gives Uriel wings, halo, flaming sword, handheld flame, armor, or crown
Genesis 3:24 does not identify Uriel as the guardian of Eden
Measured celestial order, not a modern astronomy diagram, anchors the Astronomical Book witness
Later elemental, planetary, directional, and Solomonic correspondences are excluded
artReview.style: Ancient Witness Bestiary: historically grounded narrative realism, encaustic and egg-tempera pigment character, tactile ancient materials, restrained sacred strangeness

roles: Guide of the Rebel Stars' Prison
Recorder and Leader of the Luminaries
entries.description: Enoch remembers Uriel as a guide through dangerous knowledge rather than a decorative bearer of light. He warns Noah of the flood, explains the prisons of rebel angels and burning stars, identifies the valley of judgment, and records for Enoch the exact names, portals, seasons, and 364-day courses of the heavenly lights. In 2 Esdras, Uriel answers Ezra's anguish by testing the limits of human understanding, disclosing the measured completion of the age, and finally taking the collapsed seer by the right hand to comfort and raise him.

ancientDossier.witness: Uriel joins the appeal over the Watchers' devastation, then is sent to warn Noah and preserve his seed. He leads Enoch through the chaotic prison where transgressing stars burn like mountains, interprets the abyss and accursed valley, and shows and writes the laws of the stars. Across the Astronomical Book he teaches the portals and measured courses of sun, moon, winds, seasons, and the exact year. To Ezra he is the sent examiner and interpreter who exposes what a mortal cannot measure, yet also takes the collapsed seer by the right hand and restores him.
ancientDossier.attestedTraits: Exact instruction; warning before catastrophe; guardianship and interpretation of penal cosmic regions; authority over the ordered luminaries, night, and day; willingness to challenge presumptuous questions; patient disclosure within limits; physical comfort and restoration. His light-office is cosmic and calendrical rather than an attested handheld object. Later Adam literature also makes him a participant in Adam and Abel's burial.
ancientDossier.textualBoundary: Genesis names no Uriel at Eden and assigns the flaming turning sword to no named angel. Early texts give Uriel no wings, halo, sword, flame, book, armor, complexion, or clothing color. English versions of 1 Enoch 20:2 diverge between 'world and Tartarus' and 'clamour and terror,' so the wording is not treated as uncontested. Later planetary, elemental, directional, colored, and sigilic systems are excluded from the core portrait.

entries.name: Saraqiel

artReview.scene: Saraqiel is foregrounded among the seven holy watchers at the boundary of a shadowed holding-place for spirits who sin in the spirit.
crossTextualRestraints: The text supplies an office but no individualized anatomy, costume, weapon, or narrative action
Sariêl the lunar-course teacher belongs to the fallen-teacher list and is not merged into this figure
No moon, scales, wings, halo, sword, armor, or death symbolism is used
Later magical correspondences are excluded
artReview.style: Ancient Witness Bestiary: historically grounded narrative realism, encaustic and egg-tempera pigment character, tactile ancient materials, restrained sacred strangeness

roles: One of the Seven Holy Watchers
Overseer of Spirits Who Sin in the Spirit
entries.description: 1 Enoch's sevenfold list names Saraqiel among the holy angels who watch and sets him over spirits who sin in the spirit. That terse office is the secure dossier. A different name-form, Sariêl, occurs among the rebellious teachers and is said in one translation to teach the moon's course; another translation reads Asaradel. The fallen lunar teacher is not silently merged into holy Saraqiel, and the early text does not call Saraqiel an angel of death or describe his appearance.

extraBiblical: 1 Enoch 8:3 (Sariêl/Asaradel lunar teacher is a distinct, textually unstable figure)

ancientDossier.witness: The Enochic seer gives only a roster statement: among the seven holy angels who watch, Saraqiel is set over spirits who sin in the spirit. The same corpus separately places Sariêl in the list of corrupting teachers, with the lunar course as his illicit disclosure in Charles's reading. Laurence reads Asaradel there, underscoring the instability rather than resolving it.
ancientDossier.attestedTraits: Holy-watcher status and delegated oversight concerning spiritually offending spirits. No further deed, temperament, visible form, instrument, or speech is securely attached to Saraqiel in the consulted early witness.
ancientDossier.textualBoundary: Saraqiel is not securely the fallen Sariêl, lunar teacher, angel of death, Moses' calendar instructor, or an avenger bearing scales. Suriel/Sariel/Suryal/Saraqael spellings wander across later lists and translations and are not combined automatically. The artwork's humanlike sentinel is explicitly a restrained visual inference from office, not attested anatomy.

entries.name: Raguel

artReview.scene: At the western end of the earth, Raguel explains to Enoch the unceasing regular course of fire associated with all the luminaries of heaven.
crossTextualRestraints: No scales, measuring rod, throne, armor, sword, wings, or halo is supplied
Humanlike form is a restrained visual inference rather than attested anatomy
The marked translation verbs 'takes vengeance' and 'persecutes' are treated as uncertain
Later magical correspondences are excluded
artReview.style: Ancient Witness Bestiary: historically grounded narrative realism, encaustic and egg-tempera pigment character, tactile ancient materials, restrained sacred strangeness

roles: One of the Seven Holy Watchers
Interpreter of the Unceasing Western Fire
entries.description: 1 Enoch places Raguel among the seven holy watchers and assigns him a textually difficult corrective office concerning the world of the luminaries. At the western end of the earth he answers Enoch's question about a fire that runs regularly without rest by day or night, identifying it as the western fire associated with all heaven's luminaries. This makes him an interpreter and custodian of cosmic order; it does not establish the later courtroom portrait of scales, throne, armor, or authority over every angel.

ancientDossier.witness: The sevenfold roster assigns Raguel an uncertainly worded punitive or corrective relation to the world of the luminaries. Later in Enoch's journey, Raguel is one of the holy angels with him at the western end of the earth. He explains the ceaseless, regular westward fire associated with the heavenly lights.
ancientDossier.attestedTraits: Holy-watcher status; knowledge of the luminary realm; corrective jurisdiction expressed through unstable translation; direct interpretation of witnessed cosmic fire. His concern is ordered heavenly lights, not an attested universal celestial court.
ancientDossier.textualBoundary: Charles marks both 'takes vengeance on' and 'persecutes' as uncertain readings, while Laurence phrases the passages differently. No source gives Raguel scales, measuring rod, throne, armor, wings, halo, color scheme, or bodily description. The artwork's humanlike guide is explicitly inferential.

entries.name: Remiel / Jeremiel

artReview.scene: Ramiel, who presides over true visions, interprets for Baruch the sea-cloud's alternating black and white waters and the final healing lightning.
crossTextualRestraints: No trumpet, graveyard, floating souls, wings, halo, armor, or weapon is supplied
Humanlike anatomy is a restrained inference because 2 Baruch gives no bodily description
2 Esdras 4 names Uriel, not Remiel, and is excluded from this dossier
Later Jeremiel conflations and magical correspondences are not used as visual evidence
artReview.style: Ancient Witness Bestiary: historically grounded narrative realism, encaustic and egg-tempera pigment character, tactile ancient materials, restrained sacred strangeness

roles: One of the Seven Holy Watchers
Interpreter of History's Dark and Bright Waters
entries.description: 1 Enoch names Remiel among the seven holy watchers and says God set him over those who rise. In 2 Baruch, the name-form Ramiel presides over true visions and interprets the great sea-cloud whose alternating black and white waters disclose successive ages of corruption and righteousness, ending in tribulation, illumination, and healing. The record supports resurrection oversight and truthful apocalyptic interpretation, but not the later generic portrait of a trumpet-bearing guide escorting individual souls.

ancientDossier.witness: The Enochic roster says Remiel is set by God over those who rise. Baruch's apocalypse gives Ramiel a speaking role: sent as the angel over true visions, he interprets the cloud from the sea, its twelve alternating dark and bright waters, the final black waters, and the lightning that heals the earth as the ordered history and end of the age.
ancientDossier.attestedTraits: Holy-watcher status; delegated relation to those who rise; custody of truthful visions; sustained interpretation of symbolic history; disclosure of judgment, messianic culmination, illumination, and healing. The texts emphasize intelligible interpretation rather than spectacle or psychopomp activity.
ancientDossier.textualBoundary: The righteous dead's question in 2 Esdras 4:36 is answered by Uriel, not Remiel. Remiel/Ramiel/Jeremiel name equivalence varies across later traditions. No early witness gives this angel a trumpet, wings, halo, weapon, thunderbolt, graveyard, clothing color, or bodily description.

entries.name: Metatron

artReview.scene: Before the seventh palace, Metatron recounts Enoch's transformation into a world-scale body of flame, many burning wings, and hundreds of thousands of sun-bright eyes as Rabbi Ishmael looks on.
crossTextualRestraints: The fiery multi-winged, many-eyed form belongs specifically to the late Hekhalot witness
Genesis 5 does not name Metatron or describe Enoch's transformation
Delegated divine naming is not visualized as equality with God
Metatron's Cube, occult seals, and modern sacred geometry are excluded
artReview.style: Ancient Witness Bestiary: historically grounded narrative realism, encaustic and egg-tempera pigment character, tactile ancient materials, restrained sacred strangeness intensified for the Hekhalot vision

roles: Enoch Transformed in the Hekhalot Witness
Servant of the Throne and Chariot
entries.description: 3 Enoch identifies Metatron as Enoch son of Jared transformed for service at the throne: flesh to flame, sinews to blazing fire, bones to coals, eyes to torches, hair to flame, and limbs to burning wings. He receives seventy-two world-spanning wings, 365,000 sun-bright eyes, a throne at the seventh palace, and delegated authority among heavenly households. Hagigah 15a supplies the necessary boundary: when his seated scribal office leads Elisha to imagine two powers, Metatron is punished with fiery lashes, demonstrating that even his terrifying rank remains subordinate.

ancientDossier.witness: Metatron tells Rabbi Ishmael that he was Enoch, taken from the flood generation and installed to serve the throne, chariot, and Shekinah. He narrates his transformation into blazing fire, his multiplication of wings and eyes, and his enthronement near the seventh palace. The Talmud remembers him seated to write Israel's merits, then struck with sixty fiery lashes when that privilege occasions a two-powers error.
ancientDossier.attestedTraits: Late Hekhalot testimony supplies extreme visionary anatomy: flame flesh, fiery sinews, coal bones, lightning lashes, torch eyes, burning hair, seventy-two world-covering wings, and 365,000 eyes like the Great Light. Offices include Prince of the Presence, throne servant, chariot attendant, recorder, teacher, and delegated judge. The title Youth and the name-bearing language signal proximity and commission, not independence.
ancientDossier.textualBoundary: Metatron is absent from Genesis, and Enoch's biblical taking does not itself attest this transformation. The etymology of Metatron is disputed. 'Lesser YHWH' belongs to a specific late mystical naming theology and must be read beside rabbinic rejection of two powers. Modern cubes, seals, geometric diagrams, planetary systems, and New Age claims are excluded.

entries.name: Raziel
roles: Bearer of the Book to Adam
Teacher of Mysteries in Medieval Tradition
entries.description: In the medieval Sefer Raziel tradition, Adam prays after his expulsion for understanding of his future and descendants. On the third day, beside the river from Paradise, Raziel appears carrying a sacred book, reads from it until Adam falls in fear, then commands him to rise, receive it, study it in purity, and teach the worthy. When Adam takes the book, flame rises by the river and the angel ascends. This is a medieval revelatory legend, not an episode named in Genesis.

extraBiblical: The Book of Raziel Adam legend

artReview.reason: The old generalized occult portrait does not show the card's controlling textual event and imports unattested celestial symbolism.
artReview.requiredScene: At midday beside the river flowing from Eden, a restrained humanlike messenger reads from and offers an inscribed book to frightened, kneeling Adam; a column of flame rises at the riverbank for Raziel's ascent.
exclusions: modern occult glyphs or sacred geometry
visual claim that Genesis narrates the event
artReview.style: Ancient Witness Bestiary: historically grounded narrative realism, encaustic and egg-tempera pigment character, tactile ancient materials, restrained sacred strangeness

ancientDossier.witness: The received legend speaks from Adam's exile: after his prayer for knowledge, Raziel comes on the third day in the heat beside Paradise's river, carrying and reading a book. Adam falls in terror, receives the volume at the angel's command, and sees flame rise as the messenger ascends.
ancientDossier.attestedTraits: Raziel is a commissioned revealer and bearer of a book concerned with times, future conditions, sacred knowledge, and angelic mysteries. The name is conventionally understood as 'Mystery/Secret of God,' and Sefer Raziel itself links the angel's name to transmitting mysteries to Adam. The scene supplies no extraordinary bodily anatomy.
ancientDossier.textualBoundary: Raziel is absent from Genesis, the Dead Sea Scrolls, and the early angel lists used elsewhere in this bestiary. The extant Sefer Raziel is a composite medieval work, probably compiled in the thirteenth century from earlier materials. Claims that he records every divine secret beside the throne, and modern occult diagrams attached to him, are not admitted without a controlling text.

entries.name: Angel of Death (later: Azrael)
entries.description: The Hebrew Bible and Talmud know an Angel of Death or destroying messenger but do not name him Azrael. Avodah Zarah 20b places the Angel of Death above a dying person's head with a drawn sword and a drop of poison hanging from its tip; the terrified person opens the mouth, receives the drop, dies, pales, and decays. Other rabbinic scenes show a commissioned power whose appointed deaths cannot be evaded, not a gentle modern psychopomp.

artReview.reason: The prior image and dossier treat later Azrael folklore as though it were the ancient Jewish witness and romanticize the figure as a compassionate psychopomp.
artReview.requiredScene: A late-antique sickroom: above the dying person's head an austere humanlike Angel of Death holds a drawn sword with one dark drop suspended from its point; the person sees it in terror.
exclusions: body covered in eyes and tongues
artReview.style: Ancient Witness Bestiary: historically grounded narrative realism, encaustic and egg-tempera pigment character, tactile ancient materials, restrained sacred strangeness

ancientDossier.witness: Rabbinic witnesses call the figure simply the Angel of Death. Avodah Zarah sees him poised over the sickbed with drawn sword and a fatal drop. Sukkah presents him carrying out appointed deaths despite Solomon's attempt to evade them; Shabbat remembers him disclosing to Moses how plague may be checked.
ancientDossier.attestedTraits: He acts under permission or appointment, takes life, may operate through plague, and in one teaching is identified with Satan and the evil inclination as tempter, accuser, and executioner. The sword and suspended drop are specifically attested visual attributes; compassion, a soul-separating ritual, and universal eyes-and-tongues anatomy are not.
ancientDossier.textualBoundary: Neither Tanakh nor Talmud supplies the proper name Azrael. Exodus's destroyer and the plague angel remain unnamed, and their exact identity with every later Angel-of-Death story should not be assumed. Even Qur'an 32:11 uses only the title Angel of Death. 'Azrael' is retained solely as a later catalog label.

entries.name: The Satan / The Adversary
entries.classification: Heavenly Accuser in Job; Later Devil
entries.description: Job's ha-satan comes among the sons of God as an accuser, challenges Job's motives, and can act only inside limits YHWH sets. Zechariah likewise places the accuser at the high priest's right hand and has YHWH rebuke him. A later Life of Adam and Eve gives the devil a fall narrative in his own speech: he refuses Michael's command to bow before Adam, claims seniority, seeks a seat above the stars, and is expelled with his angels. These layers must be distinguished rather than fused with Sammael or Isaiah's king of Babylon.

extraBiblical: Greek Life of Adam and Eve 12-16

artReview.reason: A generic horned demon collapses Job's subordinate court accuser into much later devil iconography.
artReview.requiredScene: Job's heavenly court: a severe humanlike accuser among the sons of God addresses overwhelming unfigured divine radiance and gestures toward Job far below.
artReview.style: Ancient Witness Bestiary: historically grounded narrative realism, encaustic and egg-tempera pigment character, tactile ancient materials, restrained sacred strangeness

ancientDossier.witness: Job sees the satan enter the divine assembly, question whether Job fears God for nothing, and receive bounded authority to test him. The Life of Adam and Eve later lets the devil explain his own exile as the result of refusing to bow before Adam and attempting self-exaltation.
ancientDossier.attestedTraits: In the Hebrew court scenes he accuses, tests, ranges through the earth, and remains subordinate to divine command. Later texts identify Satan with the devil, deceiver, ancient serpent, and defeated apocalyptic dragon, and give him angels of his own.
ancientDossier.textualBoundary: The Hebrew noun satan means adversary/accuser and is not always a proper name. Job's court officer, Chronicles' inciter, the Adam literature's expelled devil, and Revelation's dragon are related by developing tradition but not identical dossiers at every date. Isaiah 14 concerns Babylon's king; Sammael is later and excluded from the heading.

entries.name: Semyaza
entries.description: In 1 Enoch 6, Semyaza leads the two hundred children of heaven who desire human wives. He fears the others will abandon the deed and leave him alone to bear its penalty; they answer by swearing together under mutual imprecations on Mount Hermon. He teaches enchantments and root-cutting, rules his associates, joins their transgression, and later weeps with them when Enoch bears the refusal of their petition. Michael is commanded to bind Semyaza and his associates after they witness their giant sons destroy one another.

artReview.reason: Generic armored fallen-angel imagery misses the uniquely attested Hermon oath and invents anatomy, costume, and coercive command.
artReview.requiredScene: On Hermon's cold summit Semyaza stands hesitantly at the center of a great ring of humanlike heavenly beings as all extend hands and bind themselves together by oath; their ranks recede around the ridge.
artReview.style: Ancient Witness Bestiary: historically grounded narrative realism, encaustic and egg-tempera pigment character, tactile ancient materials, restrained sacred strangeness

ancientDossier.witness: Semyaza speaks as a fearful leader, warning that he may be left alone to pay for the proposed sin. His two hundred associates answer with a collective oath on Hermon. Later Enoch sees the Watchers gathered in fear, weeping with covered faces, and reports that their petition will not be granted.
ancientDossier.attestedTraits: He bears authority among the associates, participates in taking human wives, teaches enchantments and root-cutting, fathers giant offspring in later Book of Giants tradition, and is sentenced with his associates to subterranean bonds for seventy generations before final judgment.
ancientDossier.textualBoundary: Genesis names no Watcher and supplies neither Semyaza, Hermon, oath, nor teachings. The name's etymology is uncertain. The Apkallu comparison is modern scholarship, while the Ohya-Ahya genealogy is clearest in a later Manichaean branch of the Book of Giants tradition; neither may be narrated as the plain wording of Genesis.

entries.name: Azazel
roles: Teacher of Ornament, Cosmetics, Stones, and Dyes
entries.description: Leviticus sends a living goat 'for Azazel' into the wilderness bearing Israel's confessed iniquities, but gives Azazel no anatomy or biography. In 1 Enoch, Azazel teaches swords, knives, shields, breastplates, metalwork, bracelets, ornament, antimony, beautified eyelids, costly stones, and dyes. Raphael is commanded to bind him hand and foot in Dudael, cover him with jagged rocks and darkness, and hide his face from light until the great judgment.

artReview.reason: The armored warrior portrait narrows Azazel's teachings and misses the uniquely detailed Dudael binding, while risking fusion with the Levitical goat.
artReview.requiredScene: Raphael binds humanlike Azazel hand and foot in Dudael as rough jagged rocks close over him and his face is covered from light; abandoned weapons, ornaments, antimony, pigments, and stones mark his teachings.
exclusions: identifying Azazel as the Levitical goat
artReview.style: Ancient Witness Bestiary: historically grounded narrative realism, encaustic and egg-tempera pigment character, tactile ancient materials, restrained sacred strangeness

ancientDossier.witness: Leviticus witnesses the goat bearing confessed iniquities into a cut-off wilderness for Azazel. Enoch witnesses a named revealer blamed for earthly corruption, hears the sentence delivered, and tells Azazel directly that bonds and denied peace await him.
ancientDossier.attestedTraits: Azazel reveals both instruments of bloodshed and technologies of adornment: weapons, defenses, metals, jewelry, eye paint, stones, and dyes. His Enochic punishment is unusually concrete—bound hand and foot by Raphael, cast into Dudael's darkness, buried beneath jagged rocks, and denied sight of light.
ancientDossier.textualBoundary: The meaning of Azazel in Leviticus is disputed, and 'scapegoat' names the English ritual image rather than securely translating a personal name. Leviticus does not explicitly identify a Watcher. The Enochic and later Abrahamic figures must be related cautiously rather than read wholesale into the Torah.

entries.name: Lilith (Ben Sira)
roles: First Woman in the Ben Sira Tale
Party to the Three-Angel Amulet Oath
entries.description: In the medieval Alphabet of Ben Sira, God creates Lilith from earth as Adam was created. They quarrel over sexual position; she argues that they are equal because both came from earth, pronounces the Ineffable Name, and flies away. Sanoy, Sansanoy, and Semangelof find her at the sea and demand her return. She refuses; amid threats against her children and her declared danger to infants, she swears not to harm a child protected by an amulet bearing the three angels' names or forms. The episode explains a healing amulet and is not a lost Genesis account.

extraBiblical: Alphabet of Ben Sira (Alfabeta de-Ben Sira)

artReview.reason: A seductive crowned demoness imports later queen imagery and omits the Ben Sira tale's defining sea confrontation and amulet compact.
artReview.requiredScene: At the dark sea Lilith, humanlike and wind-tossed, raises a hand in refusal before the three plainly robed messenger-angels; one bears a small protective amulet with non-legible marks.
artReview.style: Ancient Witness Bestiary: historically grounded narrative realism, encaustic and egg-tempera pigment character, tactile ancient materials, restrained sacred strangeness

ancientDossier.witness: Ben Sira tells the story to explain an amulet for a sick royal child: Lilith claims equality with Adam from shared earthly formation, speaks the Ineffable Name, flees, refuses the three angels at the sea, and enters a protective oath keyed to their names and images.
ancientDossier.attestedTraits: She is earth-formed, verbally defiant, capable of flight after pronouncing the Name, associated with the sea, mother of children threatened with daily death, and a danger to infants limited by the three-angel amulet. No extraordinary physical anatomy is described.
ancientDossier.textualBoundary: This anonymous medieval, frequently comic and transgressive work is not the biblical Ben Sira/Sirach and is not evidence of a suppressed Genesis wife. The text says she pronounced the Name, not that God gave it to her alongside Adam. Demon queenship, covenant philosophy, and modern ideological readings are excluded from the eyewitness-facing dossier.

entries.name: Lilith (Isaiah 34)
entries.description: Isaiah 34:14 places the singular feminine lilith within Edom after judgment: among ruined palaces overgrown by thorns, jackals and desert creatures meet, a goat-being calls to its fellow, and there Lilith settles and finds herself a resting place. The following lines gather a nesting snake and paired birds under divine command. The verse gives Lilith no ancestry, speech, attack, or anatomy; she is an uncanny inhabitant within the poem's complete desolation ecology, not Adam's wife or a demon queen.

artReview.reason: A glamorous demoness portrait overwhelms Isaiah's actual subject: a gathered ecology occupying judged Edom, in which Lilith is only one resting presence.
artReview.requiredScene: Moonlit ruined Edomite fortifications overgrown by thorns, populated by jackals, desert birds, a goat-being, snake nest, and raptors; an elusive humanlike female night presence rests within a collapsed chamber threshold.
artReview.style: Ancient Witness Bestiary: historically grounded narrative realism, encaustic and egg-tempera pigment character, tactile ancient materials, restrained sacred strangeness

ancientDossier.witness: The prophet sees Edom emptied of rulers and human habitation, its defenses overtaken by thorn. The commanded creatures receive it as an enduring allotment; among them the singular Lilith settles and finds her own resting place.
ancientDossier.attestedTraits: Lilith is grammatically feminine, associated with ruined wilderness habitation, and at rest rather than attacking. Her neighbors—jackals/desert creatures, goat-being, nesting snake, and paired birds—define the scene more securely than any proposed bodily form.
ancientDossier.textualBoundary: This is the only biblical occurrence of לִילִית. A relationship with Mesopotamian lilītu traditions is plausible but does not import their whole dossier. Isaiah supplies no Adam story, infant threat, amulet, queenship, speech, flight, sexuality, or exact anatomy; those belong to other textual layers.

entries.name: Lilith in 4Q510
entries.classification: Named Spirit in an Apotropaic Song
roles: One Presence among the Hostile Spirits
entries.description: In 4Q510 fragment 1, the Maskil proclaims God's glorious splendor to frighten and terrify a company of hostile spirits: ravaging angels, spirits of the bastards, demons, singular Lilith, howlers, desert beings, and attackers who strike without warning. Lilith receives no separate biography or anatomy. The song places her inside the present, bounded dominion of wickedness and opposes that company with divine radiance and the spirit of understanding.

artReview.reason: The manuscript's scene is the Maskil's divine praise driving back a mixed company of spirits, not plural wind-demonesses attacking childbirth.
artReview.requiredScene: A Qumran Maskil proclaims a hymn in a lamplit desert cave as restrained divine radiance presses ravaging spirits, demons, a howler, desert forms, and one elusive female-associated night presence back into darkness.
artReview.style: Ancient Witness Bestiary: historically grounded narrative realism, encaustic and egg-tempera pigment character, tactile ancient materials, restrained sacred strangeness

ancientDossier.witness: The Maskil proclaims the splendor of God in order to terrify the hostile company that stalks the age of wickedness; singular Lilith stands named among demons, bastard spirits, howlers, desert beings, and sudden assailants.
ancientDossier.attestedTraits: Lilith belongs to a mixed hostile company opposed to divine radiance and the spirit of understanding. The surviving fragment attests her name and placement, but supplies no appearance, speech, origin, victims, or individual deed.
ancientDossier.textualBoundary: The Hebrew is singular לילית. Childbirth, infants, sexuality, plural wind-demonesses, Adam, queenship, and a narrated binding are absent. Mesopotamian parallels and later Jewish protective traditions must remain outside this Qumran dossier.

entries.name: Lilith
entries.description: This is a concordance, not a fourth biography. Isaiah 34:14 places singular Lilith at rest within ruined Edom's wilderness company. 4Q510 names singular Lilith among hostile spirits terrified by the Maskil's praise. The medieval Alphabet of Ben Sira gives Lilith an Adam narrative and an oath-confrontation with three angels beside the sea. Each witness has its own card; no single ancient text joins all three dossiers.

artReview.reason: A single demoness portrait falsely fuses three texts separated by genre and centuries.
artReview.requiredScene: A clearly divided three-panel ancient concordance: Lilith resting in ruined Edom; the Qumran Maskil's radiance driving back a mixed spirit company; and the Ben Sira sea-oath confrontation with exactly three angels.
artReview.style: Ancient Witness Bestiary: historically grounded narrative realism, encaustic and egg-tempera pigment character, tactile ancient materials, restrained sacred strangeness

ancientDossier.witness: The name is preserved in three different textual scenes: rest in Edom, opposition to the Maskil's praise, and a medieval sea-oath narrative after departure from Adam.
ancientDossier.attestedTraits: Only singular grammatical identity is shared securely between Isaiah and 4Q510; Ben Sira reuses the name in a developed narrative. The dedicated cards preserve what each witness actually attests.
ancientDossier.textualBoundary: No ancient witness combines Edom, Qumran's spirit catalogue, Adam, infant threat, demon queenship, succubus lore, and modern archetypal interpretation. Mesopotamian comparanda explain possibilities in transmission, not a continuous biography.

entries.name: Asmodeus
roles: Driven to Egypt and Bound by Raphael
entries.description: Asmodeus is the evil spirit who killed Sarah's seven husbands before they consummated their marriages. Raphael instructs Tobias to burn a fish's heart and liver upon incense ash; Asmodeus smells the smoke, flees from the marriage chamber to the far parts of Egypt, and is pursued and bound by Raphael. Tobit gives him no royal title, fixed anatomy, or general office as a demon of lust.

artReview.reason: Later demon-king and grimoire iconography obscures Tobit's actual marriage-chamber expulsion and supplies anatomy the book never gives.
artReview.requiredScene: Tobias burns the fish heart and liver on incense ash while Sarah prays; the smoke drives one unresolved dark spirit through the doorway toward Egypt as Raphael pursues in restrained angelic radiance.
artReview.style: Ancient Witness Bestiary: historically grounded narrative realism, encaustic and egg-tempera pigment character, tactile ancient materials, restrained sacred strangeness

ancientDossier.witness: Sarah's seven bridegrooms die before consummation. At Raphael's instruction Tobias burns a fish's heart and liver; the spirit flees to Egypt, Raphael binds him, and the newlyweds turn to prayer.
ancientDossier.attestedTraits: Asmodeus is named an evil spirit, lethal to Sarah's husbands, repelled by the prescribed smoke, capable of flight to a distant region, and subject to Raphael's restraint.
ancientDossier.textualBoundary: Tobit does not call him king, personified lust, or rage; it supplies no body. The Testament of Solomon later makes him a self-described enemy of newlyweds and adulterous instigator, while Gittin 68 calls Ashmedai king of demons in a separate shamir story. Grimoire ranks and composite anatomy are later still.

entries.name: Belial
entries.classification: Ruler of the Dark Lot at Qumran
roles: Commander of the Army of Darkness
Ruler over Spirits of His Lot
entries.description: In older Hebrew idiom, belial denotes worthlessness, lawlessness, or ruin; 'sons of Belial' are wicked people, not a demon's offspring. At Qumran the term becomes unmistakably personal: Belial rules the dark lot and its spirits, and his army opposes the Sons of Light in the War Scroll. His dominion is appointed and temporary; God destroys it in the decisive lot of battle.

artReview.reason: A crowned demon prince imports later grimoire anatomy; the War Scroll depicts Belial through his lot, spirits, army, dark dominion, and coming defeat.
artReview.requiredScene: Across a Judean valley, ordered Sons of Light face Belial's human army of darkness; an immense unresolved angelic shadow hangs behind the dark host while divine dawn reaches the light camp.
artReview.style: Ancient Witness Bestiary: historically grounded narrative realism, encaustic and egg-tempera pigment character, tactile ancient materials, restrained sacred strangeness

ancientDossier.witness: The War Scroll sees Belial's army and the spirits of his lot assembled against the Sons of Light. The priests curse Belial, praise God's ancient appointment of the Prince of Light, and await God's decisive overthrow of darkness.
ancientDossier.attestedTraits: Belial is personalized as a hostile angelic ruler whose dominion is darkness and whose lot includes spirits and human forces. He leads astray and wages appointed war, but remains bounded by God's times and judgment.
ancientDossier.textualBoundary: Most Hebrew Bible occurrences are idiomatic worthlessness or lawlessness, not a personal demon. Qumran supplies no body, throne, crown, fiery chariot, seal, or legions counted by number; those images belong to much later magical literature.

entries.name: Gilgamesh and Ḥobabish
entries.classification: Named Giants in Fragmentary Aramaic Witnesses
entries.description: The Aramaic Book of Giants preserves Gilgamesh and Ḥobabish by name in broken narrative witnesses. Ohyah reports words spoken by Gilgamesh; Ḥobabish raises a roar, and judgment language follows. The wider work gathers terrified giants around dreams and Enoch's oracle, but the fragments do not call this Gilgamesh king of Uruk, identify his father, recount a Cedar Forest battle, or give either figure a complete biography. Their names evoke the Babylonian Gilgamesh and Humbaba traditions without importing the whole Epic.

artReview.reason: Uruk hero imagery or Cedar Forest combat would fill Qumran's lacunae with a different composition; the surviving scene is a giant assembly under ominous judgment.
artReview.requiredScene: In an antediluvian giant assembly, Gilgamesh speaks urgently to Ohyah while Ḥobabish roars; above them a dream-sign of uprooted trees and flood-shadow foretells judgment.
artReview.style: Ancient Witness Bestiary: historically grounded narrative realism, encaustic and egg-tempera pigment character, tactile ancient materials, restrained sacred strangeness

ancientDossier.witness: Ohyah makes known what Gilgamesh said; Ḥobabish raises a roar, and the damaged assembly text turns toward judgment. Elsewhere the giants' dreams and Enoch's answer announce destruction.
ancientDossier.attestedTraits: Both are named within the Book of Giants' company. Gilgamesh speaks to Ohyah; Ḥobabish is associated with a roar in a broken sequence. Their giant setting is secure, but individual motives, deeds, parentage, and bodies are not.
ancientDossier.textualBoundary: The Babylonian Epic supplies a king of Uruk and a Cedar Forest guardian named Humbaba, but Qumran does not retell that whole plot. It does not say Gilgamesh knowingly refused repentance, make Ḥobabish his companion, or call either Semyaza's son.

entries.name: Armaros
roles: Teacher of the Resolving of Enchantments
entries.description: In Enoch's list of the descending Watchers, Armaros is a chief over ten and is charged with teaching the resolving of enchantments.

ancientDossier.witness: The Enochic narrator names Armaros among the leaders bound by the oath on Hermon, then assigns to him one forbidden instruction: how enchantments are undone.
ancientDossier.attestedTraits: He is a Watcher leader and teacher. The text associates him with counter-enchantment, not with a described body, weapon, seal, or later demonic office.
ancientDossier.textualBoundary: No surviving early passage supplies his appearance or an individual episode beyond the roster and teaching list. Solomonic ranks and modern elemental assignments are not part of this record.

artReview.reason: A generic armored fallen angel does not depict Armaros's sole individual attestation: instruction in resolving enchantments.
artReview.requiredScene: A plain humanlike Watcher shows ancient pupils how a knotted cord-and-herb binding is loosened on a flat stone below Hermon's ridge.
artReview.style: Ancient Witness Bestiary: historically grounded narrative realism, encaustic and egg-tempera pigment character, tactile ancient materials, restrained sacred strangeness

entries.name: Baraqel
entries.description: Baraqel is named among the Watcher chiefs, and the Book of Enoch remembers him as the one who taught the signs read by astrologers.

ancientDossier.witness: Enoch's account places Baraqel under the Hermon oath and names his disclosure as astrology—the reading of heavenly signs as forbidden instruction.
ancientDossier.attestedTraits: Named Watcher chief; revealer of astrological knowledge. His name contains baraq, lightning, but the narrative does not say that he commands lightning.
ancientDossier.textualBoundary: The Book of Giants' Baraqel is named as Mahaway's father, but neither that notice nor the teaching list describes wings, lightning command, or a personal battle history. Such details must not be promoted from the name alone.

artReview.reason: Generic lightning-warrior art mistakes the name's baraq element for an attested power and ignores Baraqel's assigned disclosure of astrological knowledge.
artReview.requiredScene: Below Hermon at night, a plain humanlike Watcher teaches ancient pupils to correlate star and planet paths using movable unmarked stones on dark cloth.
exclusions: planet or star held in hand
artReview.style: Ancient Witness Bestiary: historically grounded narrative realism, encaustic and egg-tempera pigment character, tactile ancient materials, restrained sacred strangeness

entries.name: Kokabiel
entries.description: Kokabiel belongs to the chiefs of the two hundred Watchers and is remembered as the revealer of the constellations.

ancientDossier.witness: The Book of the Watchers lists Kokabiel among the chiefs and attributes instruction concerning the constellations to him.
ancientDossier.attestedTraits: Watcher authority and illicit celestial instruction are explicit. The star element is present both in the name and assigned teaching.
ancientDossier.textualBoundary: The text gives no colors, armor, weapon, planetary throne, or combat power. Visual art should show an ancient celestial instructor without inventing a modern zodiac magician.

artReview.reason: A cosmic warrior or zodiac magician supplies powers and iconography absent from Kokabiel's brief constellation-teacher witness.
artReview.requiredScene: Under the open sky, a plain humanlike Watcher teaches pupils to recognize one star grouping using sighting poles, a reflecting water bowl, and counting cords, without drawn lines.
exclusions: star crown or stars in hands
artReview.style: Ancient Witness Bestiary: historically grounded narrative realism, encaustic and egg-tempera pigment character, tactile ancient materials, restrained sacred strangeness

entries.name: Penemue
entries.description: Penemue taught humankind writing with ink and paper and instructed them in bitter and sweet and the secrets of wisdom.

ancientDossier.witness: The Enochic indictment says Penemue showed human beings writing with ink and paper. The narrator treats this disclosure as a path by which many went astray, and also credits him with teaching bitter and sweet and wisdom's secrets.
ancientDossier.attestedTraits: Revealer of literacy and secret knowledge; a corrupting instructor rather than a battlefield figure in the surviving account.
ancientDossier.textualBoundary: The passage condemns the use and disclosure described by its narrator; it does not support the modern claim that writing itself originated historically with a single supernatural teacher.

artReview.reason: A generic fallen scholar misses the material disclosure of ink-and-sheet writing and the narrator's immediate warning about its corrupt use.
artReview.requiredScene: By lamplight Penemue teaches ink-making and non-linguistic practice strokes; nearby bitter herbs and honey embody the paired lesson, while a background tally deception foreshadows misuse.
artReview.style: Ancient Witness Bestiary: historically grounded narrative realism, encaustic and egg-tempera pigment character, tactile ancient materials, restrained sacred strangeness

entries.name: Kasdeja
entries.description: Kasdeja is accused of showing humankind destructive workings of spirits and demons, the striking of the embryo, and the bite of the serpent.

ancientDossier.witness: Enoch's later list assigns Kasdeja knowledge of malignant blows: attacks of spirits and demons, harm to the unborn, and the serpent's bite.
ancientDossier.attestedTraits: A revealer of occult injury and hostile spiritual practice. The testimony concerns what he taught, not a catalog of innate spell-like powers.
ancientDossier.textualBoundary: No early description gives his face, animal form, rank among Solomonic demons, or a complete pharmacology. The difficult wording should remain difficult rather than being expanded into modern lore.

entries.name: Gadreel
entries.description: One Enochic tradition names Gadreel as the being who led Eve astray and taught mortals the weapons of death.

ancientDossier.witness: The Enochic narrator identifies Gadreel—not Azazel or Satan in this passage—as Eve's deceiver, and says he showed the children of men shield, breastplate, sword, and every weapon of death.
ancientDossier.attestedTraits: Deception and weapon instruction are explicit; the bloodshed of earth is laid at his door.
ancientDossier.textualBoundary: Genesis itself does not name its serpent Gadreel. This is a later Enochic identification and must remain labeled as such, not harmonized into a single biography of Satan.

entries.name: Mastema
entries.description: In Jubilees, Mastema petitions to retain a tenth of the corrupt spirits under his authority so that they may exercise judgment and lead the guilty astray.

ancientDossier.witness: Jubilees presents the prince Mastema speaking before God. When Noah asks relief from unclean spirits, Mastema argues that some be left under his rule; nine parts are bound and one part remains. He later presses the testing of Abraham and opposes Moses.
ancientDossier.attestedTraits: He commands a limited remnant of spirits, accuses, tests, and obstructs. His activity occurs by sufferance and under limits, not as an equal rival sovereign.
ancientDossier.textualBoundary: Jubilees does not give Mastema horns, a seal, or a Solomonic legion number. Equating him completely with Satan is an interpretation, though the functions overlap.

entries.name: Abaddon / Apollyon
entries.description: The Apocalypse names the king over the abyssal locust host: Abaddon in Hebrew and Apollyon in Greek.

ancientDossier.witness: In older Hebrew wisdom texts, Abaddon is the realm or condition of destruction paired with Sheol. Revelation 9 personifies the name as the angelic king over creatures released from the abyss.
ancientDossier.attestedTraits: Kingship over the locust host and association with the abyss are explicit. The locusts torment for five months and do not kill; their elaborate appearance belongs to the host, not automatically to their king.
ancientDossier.textualBoundary: The witness calls him an angel, without explicitly calling him fallen or a demon. Later demonological rank, armor, and biography are absent.

entries.name: Prince of Persia
entries.translation: Prince of the Kingdom of Persia
entries.description: Daniel's heavenly messenger reports that the prince of Persia resisted him for twenty-one days until Michael came to help.

ancientDossier.witness: A radiant messenger tells Daniel that Persia's prince withstood him twenty-one days. Michael, one of the chief princes, intervened; the messenger expects to contend again with Persia's prince and then with the prince of Greece.
ancientDossier.attestedTraits: Territorial association, prolonged resistance to a heavenly messenger, and conflict with Michael are explicit. The being is powerful enough to delay but not finally prevent the message.
ancientDossier.textualBoundary: Daniel supplies no personal name, face, weapon, genealogy, or moral origin story. Calling this prince a demon is a classification inferred from opposition, not the wording of the vision.

entries.name: Behemoth
roles: Mighty Creature of the Dry Land
entries.description: God's speech to Job describes Behemoth as a grass-eating creature of immense strength; Enoch's vision places the male monster in the eastern wilderness.

ancientDossier.witness: Job is told to behold Behemoth, made by God as Job was: it eats grass, has strength in loins and belly, bones like bronze and iron, shelters among reeds, and is untroubled by the river. Enoch sees it separated from Leviathan and assigned to dry wilderness.
ancientDossier.attestedTraits: Colossal bodily strength, herbivory, riverine shelter, divine creaturehood, and later eschatological preservation are attested across the texts.
ancientDossier.textualBoundary: Job does not identify a modern animal species, nor does it call Behemoth demonic. Enoch calls it male; visual details beyond the passages remain artistic inference.

entries.name: Leviathan
entries.description: Leviathan is the unmasterable sea creature of Job, the twisting serpent punished in Isaiah, and the female monster assigned to the ocean abyss in Enoch's vision.

ancientDossier.witness: Job's divine speech describes a creature no human can leash: armored scales, terrifying teeth, fiery and smoky breath, a wake that makes the deep seem hoary, and fearlessness before weapons. Isaiah names swift and twisting Leviathan and foretells its punishment. Enoch locates the female monster in the ocean abyss.
ancientDossier.attestedTraits: Aquatic habitation, serpentine language, extraordinary armor and force, smoke and flame imagery, and subjection to God are explicit.
ancientDossier.textualBoundary: The passages do not require a medieval dragon anatomy or identify Leviathan with Satan. Enoch's sex assignment belongs to that textual tradition and should not be retrojected into Job.

entries.name: Rephaim — The Shades
entries.translation: Rephaim; later used of the departed shades
entries.description: Hebrew witnesses use Rephaim both for formidable ancient peoples and for the powerless dead who stir in Sheol; this card records the latter usage without collapsing it into the living clans.

ancientDossier.witness: The shades tremble beneath the waters in Job; they do not rise to praise in Psalm 88; Isaiah pictures Sheol rousing the Rephaim, the former leaders of the earth, to greet a fallen king. Isaiah 26 contrasts dead Rephaim who do not rise with God's dead who shall live.
ancientDossier.attestedTraits: They belong to the underworld and are portrayed as diminished dead, retaining identity and royal memory but lacking the vitality of the living giant clans.
ancientDossier.textualBoundary: The Hebrew texts do not depict these shades as game-style necromancers or prove that every dead human becomes a Rephaim. The relationship between Ugaritic ancestral rpum and biblical usage is comparative evidence, not an eyewitness identification.
